articles.title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
articles.summary: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. Via Hacker News Tags: iframes , javascript , sandboxing , security , xss , openai , chatgpt , content-security-policy

articles.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
articles.summary: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. articles.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
articles.summary: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

articles.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
articles.summary: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. articles.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
articles.summary: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance. I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here's the chat transcript that built it. It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here's that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here's that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here's that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave". Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well. Battle Drones This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season. I called it "Quarter Sun Cove". I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off. Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you. It's absurdly cute. You can play the latest version here . I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors. Here's the initial brainstorming session , which resulted in this spec file . Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it. I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true. This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times. Four times as insulting If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once . I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself. The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve's Steam Next Fest is a good recent example. We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don't suck! Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone! I expect that, as we've already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction! I certainly won't be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don't feel like I've earned that right. We'll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects. What happens if someone actually puts the work in? The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input . The projects I've described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I've put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself). Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it's as good as they can make it. I want to see games that wouldn't have existed without these new tools. You should build a game! Building games in this way is so much fun . It's the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project? (OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache !) All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers - including mobile browsers - are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser . I'm finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I'm trying to build. I suggest starting with a prompt like this: Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where... This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai - you don't even need to fire up a full coding agent. As one last example, here's "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat" by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High . Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase. And if the game isn't fun enough, add this: Make it a LOT more fun Tags: game-design , games , ai , generative-ai , chatgpt , llms , claude , vibe-coding , claude-code

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
articles.summary: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. articles.title: Introducing Geist Serif
articles.summary: Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.Same system, new voiceAt Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.Display firstGeist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.From the first prototype to todayThe first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.Geist grew teethThe goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”Four families, one x-heightGeist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.MetricGeist SansGeist SerifUPM10001000Cap height710710x-height530530Ascender710750Descender-150-200Four variants, one axisLike Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:Crafted by handIn July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.Specs at a glanceGeist Serif ships with:1 weight (Regular)4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)894 glyphs5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)352 supported languagesGetting startedGeist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:Exports and CSS variables:GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serifGeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regularGeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-squareGeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangleGeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heartEach one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.What’s nextRegular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.Weights from Thin to BlackThe variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.Toward a text faceTo explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.Italics, built rule by ruleWe’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.More scripts and Google FontsCyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.One familyWith Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.Download Geist Serif and start building.Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you. Read more

articles.title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
articles.summary: Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.Why we built Runtime CacheData Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.How Runtime Cache worksThe infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.What we’ve shippedFaster reads during traffic burstsChecking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.More storage and fewer evictionsWe raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.More visibility into cache behaviorWe’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.Bringing Data Cache into Runtime CacheWe’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes. Read more
